Group a GPU table by one or more columns

Source: R/group-by.R
group_by.tbl_gpu.Rd

Marks columns to group by for subsequent operations like summarise(). The grouping is stored as metadata and does not perform any computation until an aggregation is requested.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
group_by(.data, ..., .add = FALSE, .drop = dplyr::group_by_drop_default(.data))

Arguments

.data

A tbl_gpu object created by tbl_gpu().

...

Variables to group by: column names (x, .data$x), a top-level dplyr::pick(), or computed columns (name = expression, or an unnamed expression such as a + 1; see "Computed groups" below). Like dplyr, tidyselect helpers are only allowed inside pick().

.add

If FALSE (default), will override existing groups. If TRUE, will add to existing groups.

.drop

Whether to drop unobserved factor-level combinations from group_data()/group_keys()/n_groups()/etc. Defaults to group_by_drop_default(.data): TRUE for an ungrouped table, the table's current setting for a grouped one (as in dplyr). See ".drop semantics" below for the exact scope of what's honored.

Value

A grouped tbl_gpu object. The object has the same data but with grouping columns recorded for use by summarise().

Details

Unlike operations like dplyr::filter() or mutate(), group_by() does not perform any expensive GPU aggregation itself. It simply records which columns should be used for grouping in subsequent aggregation operations (computed group columns, see below, DO run a real mutate()).

The actual groupby computation happens when you call summarise() (or one of the group_data() family) on the grouped table. This lazy approach allows you to chain multiple operations before executing the expensive groupby operation.

Computed groups

Verified empirically against dplyr 1.2.1: a named argument (e.g. group_by(df, g = x %/% 2), or even a bare-symbol rename like group_by(df, g = x)) is ALWAYS treated as a mutate() expression – the original column (if any) is kept, a new (or overwritten) column is added under the given name, and the table is then grouped by that name. Later dots may reference earlier dots' newly-computed columns, exactly like mutate()'s own chain semantics (e.g. group_by(df, g = x %/% 2, h = g * 10)). An unnamed argument is a column reference (x, .data$x, .data[["x"]]), which names an existing column, a top-level pick(), which adds the columns it selects, or – anything else – a data-masking expression computed into a new column named rlang::as_label() of the expression (group_by(df, a + 1) makes a column called a + 1). As soon as one dot is named or is not a column reference (a pick() or a NULL counts), every dot is data-masking, so a bare name that is not a column (a variable in the calling environment) is computed too, as in mutate(). All computed dots (named and unnamed) run as one mutate() on the ungrouped data, in argument order. Every dot's resulting group column name(s) are combined in the order the arguments were written. The old add = and .dots = arguments are defunct and error.

Calling group_by() with no arguments and .add = FALSE (the default) clears any existing grouping entirely (verified empirically – this differs from simply returning .data unchanged, which was this function's historical, incorrect behavior for that case).

.drop semantics

.drop = FALSE (verified empirically against dplyr 1.2.1) adds one placeholder row (.rows = integer(0)) to group_data()'s output for every declared factor level combination of the FACTOR grouping columns that has no observed row, expanded recursively like dplyr: under each parent group a factor column takes all its levels (plus NA if observed there) and a non-factor column the values observed under that parent (a single NA under an empty parent); see expand_dropped_groups().

.drop is stored as a single boolean on the returned tbl_gpu ($group_drop) and carried by push_op()/push_join() through every verb that keeps a group column (and by count(), add_count() and slice_sample(), which build their result directly); it is reset to TRUE once no group column is left. Like dplyr, .drop defaults to the table's current setting, so regrouping a .drop = FALSE table keeps it.

Groups are recomputed from the data each time, and empty factor-level groups are re-added from the declared levels. Row-subsetting verbs also keep emptied groups of any key type, as dplyr does. On a .drop = FALSE table, filter(), filter_out(), slice(), slice_head(), slice_tail(), slice_min(), slice_max(), slice_sample(), semi_join(), anti_join() and rows_delete() keep every group, emptied ones included. .preserve = TRUE does the same for slice() and filter() on a .drop = TRUE table. The result fixes the input's group-keys table ($fixed_keys), only when a group can have been lost, which group_data() and friends, collect(), summarise()/count()/ tally() (on the GPU, with a row for each emptied group) and the CPU fallbacks honour. mutate(), select(), rename() and relocate() carry it as long as they leave the group columns alone, and a CPU fallback result carries whatever empty groups dplyr's own result kept (see gpu_fallback(): a fallback mutate() keeps them, a fallback arrange() on a .drop = TRUE table drops them); every other verb, and any change of grouping, drops it.

See also

summarise.tbl_gpu for aggregating grouped data, ungroup.tbl_gpu for removing grouping, group_data.tbl_gpu for the grouping metadata query family

Examples

library(dplyr)
if (has_gpu()) {
  gpu_mtcars <- tbl_gpu(mtcars)

  # Group by a single column
  by_cyl <- gpu_mtcars |>
    group_by(cyl)

  # Group by multiple columns
  by_cyl_gear <- gpu_mtcars |>
    group_by(cyl, gear)

  # Computed group column
  by_half_cyl <- gpu_mtcars |>
    group_by(half_cyl = cyl %/% 2)

  # Use with summarise for aggregation
  result <- gpu_mtcars |>
    group_by(cyl) |>
    summarise(mean_mpg = mean(mpg)) |>
    collect()
}
